Both allow us to see how a variable spreads across its range—where the mass of the data is and whether there are outliers. The curve is estimated using kernel density estimation, with a small width and a Gaussian kernel being the most widely used. Other kernel choices are available for density plots. In fact, with visualization, multiple distributions can be analyzed by identifying a response variable and one or more grouping variables. Here, the response variable is the variable of interest, while the grouping variables divide the data into subsets with distinct distributions of the response variable. The example above (Figure 14) comes from an experiment where participants were asked to estimate what share of taxes is raised by the central versus the regional government, with the treatment group provided information about the tax autonomy of regional governments (the true answer being 50%) (Foremny, 2024). Plotting the distribution of the treatment effects for different groups helps show if the treatment had an effect conditional on the pre-treatment bias. Visualizing Correlations or Relationships To visualize the relationship between two variables, it is very useful to use scatterplots or, increasingly, binned scatterplots. The binscatter is a simple yet powerful tool: Unlike traditional scatter plots, binscatter plots group observations into bins based on the values of one of the variables. The bins are usually equally spaced intervals, and the observations within each bin are summarized using a chosen statistic, such as the mean or median. Take an example from Cattaneo et al. (2022). Figure 15 presents the usual scatter plot. Then in Figure 16, the scatterplot is binned, and, within each bin, an average is calculated. Finally, Figure 17 presents the binned scatter plot, along with a polynomial fit. Binscatter plots are particularly useful when the relationship between variables is nonlinear or when many observations overlap in a traditional scatter plot, making it difficult to discern patterns. By grouping the observations into bins, binscatter plots can reveal patterns that might be obscured in a traditional scatter plot, especially when there is heteroscedasticity or clustering of the observations. (a) A Scatterplot (b) Partition & Bin Means (c) Means & Polynomial Fit Figure 13. Example of Correlation Illustration 3) Some Basic Principles for Data Visualization Keep it simple: Avoid too many colors, shapes, or design elements that distract from the data. Label axes clearly and accurately, and Label each bar with the actual data value. Order bars appropriately in logical order: This might be by size, alphabetical order, or chronological order. Use appropriate scales. If the data varies widely, consider using a logarithmic scale. Minimize clutter: Remove unnecessary gridlines or borders, and keep enough space in between bars. Use appropriate color: Use easy-to-differentiate colors to highlight key information and differences. Use annotations: Titles, subtitles, and footnotes, or a data source.

title: Visualizing Economic Research
text: After discussing how to visualize the data itself, let’s now turn to something that economists often overlook: how to visualize the results of our econometric models. 1) Tables and Graphs: A Balance Historically, regression results were shown in tables. Traditionally, we have relied on tables to report dozens of coefficients, standard errors, and significance stars. Plots can make our results much more transparent, interpretable, and convincing, especially with large data sets, modern econometric tools, and larger computational power that together provide a good base for graphical visualization of econometric results. Graphs complement, not replace, tables, in presenting results. There is a trade-off between using graphs and tables: graphs show more details, but tables allow for comparing different models and summarizing in a few parameters. Our goal is to find a balance between the two. In many cases, you can always show visuals in the main text, and report details of your estimates in tables in the appendix. In the rest of this section, we’ll review a few visualization tools that may be the most useful in applied research: binscatter and panel data, marginal effect and marginsplot, dynamic difference in differences and coefplot, robustness checks and speccurves. Binscatter and Panel Data As discussed in Section 0.2.2, binned scatterplot, or binscatter, provides a flexible, parsimonious way of visualizing simple relationships in data based on regression techniques. For presenting results, binscatter plots are also an important tool to visualize panel-data models, as it allows us to residualize on fixed effects and controls. (a) Baseline Regression (b) With State and Time FEs (c) Controlling for Population Figure 14. Using Binned Scatterplot for Panel Data Regressions For example, Ferraz, Foremny, and Santini (2024) study the relationship between tax revenues and transfers in Brazil. Figure 22 shows how the binned scatterplots visualize different regression results, and help the understanding of how the relationship of interest changes as the regression evolves. The first subplot 19 presents the baseline regression, where there seems to be a negative and non-linear relationship. With state and time fixed effects, the non-linearity between X and Y reduces, as in subplot 20. Finally, controlling for population resolves the non-linearity, as is shown in subplot 21. Here are some recommended practices when using binned scatterplots: Choose an appropriate number of bins: too few hides patterns, too many creates noise. Overlay the raw data or jittered points for transparency. Add fitted trends when appropriate. Adjust for covariates: consider residualizing variables if controlling for other factors. Label axes clearly and include units. Keep styles and scales consistent across related graphs. Plotting Marginal Effects Plotting marginal effects is especially useful in nonlinear models (logit, probit) or whenever the model includes interaction terms and the effect of a variable depends on other covariates. In such cases, raw coefficients can be misleading because they represent partial derivatives evaluated at a point, and single reported coefficients alone do not capture how the effect changes across levels of interacting variables. By plotting the predicted effect of a treatment or variable over the range of another covariate, we can see where the effect is strong, weak, or statistically insignificant. Confidence intervals provide a visual representation of uncertainty that is far more intuitive than asterisks in a table. For instance, in Foremny (2024), the treatment dummy interacts with the perceived size of the public sector. Plotting the marginal effects of the treatment across the distribution of public-sector size reveals heterogeneity and illustrates where in the public sector size variable distribution the effects originate from (Figure 25). Results Table Plotting Marginal Effects Figure 15. Marginal Effects Here are some recommended practices for marginal effects plots: Always visualize interactions or nonlinear effects. Include confidence intervals and coefficients in the plot. Plot over meaningful data ranges (avoid extrapolation). Highlight non-linearities or turning points. Label axes clearly and maintain consistent aesthetics. Combine plots with tables when necessary. Event Studies Event study graphs have become the standard way of presenting dynamic difference-in-differences results. They provide more comprehensive and nuanced insights into the impact of an event, allow for the examination of the timing and duration of the effect, as well as any potential delayed or cumulative effects, and provide a test for pre-trends. Here are some recommended practices for event study graphs: Normalize the event time: set the treatment period to 0 (except for the staggered approach). Show cumulative effects. Include confidence bands for transparency. For full transparency, include a graph (at least in the appendix) distinguishing treated vs control units, or pre- vs post-event periods. Use interpretable scales (percentage changes, deviations from baseline). Keep axes and styles consistent across related plots. Specification Curve Analysis & Research Reproducibility Finally, there is a powerful but still underused tool: the Specification Curve Analysis (SCA), proposed by Simonsohn, Simmons, and Nelson (2015). It helps address one of the main challenges in empirical research: many published studies cannot be replicated, often due to insufficient methodological details. Empirical research allows many choices in data cleaning, variable transformations, and model specification, which can influence reported effects. Small researcher decisions (e.g., excluding observations, choosing covariates) can cumulatively favor a desired narrative. Instead of presenting just one preferred specification, SCA visualizes all of them. Figure 16. A Specification Curve Figure 26 shows an example from Ferraz, Foremny, and Santini (2025). In the specification curve, each model is represented by a point on the x-axis, ordered by some criterion (for example, the estimated coefficient of interest), and the y-axis shows the value of that estimate. Such a curve represents the distribution of estimated effects across a range of model specifications and provides an overall picture of the sensitivity of the results to modeling choices. Besides, if it is about including different controls and their impact, ordering by coefficient size can show which variables or sets of them shift the point estimate of the variable of interest. The specification curve is very cool but rarely used in applied economics papers. We should use it more, as it helps with: Robustness: By considering a range of plausible specifications, a specification curve can help identify which results are most robust and not highly dependent on a particular modeling choice. Transparency: The curve provides a clear and concise visual representation of the sensitivity of the results to different model specifications, making it easier to communicate the findings to others. Efficiency: The curve can help researchers to focus on the most robust and reliable results, thereby reducing the need for time-consuming and resource-intensive sensitivity analyses. Here are some recommended practices when using specification curves: Define a clear set of plausible specifications in advance. Visualize all results, including those not shown in the paper. Report deviations from the planned analysis. Highlight influential choices and show which variables drive large changes. Use the curve to discuss robustness, not just to display it. Main Takeaways from Part 2: Visualizing econometric results is not an optional embellishment; it is part of rigorous empirical practice. Figures help readers clearly see the data, the logic of identification, the patterns behind coefficients, and the robustness of findings. They make our work more transparent and reproducible, and they allow audiences outside academia to understand what our research means.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Lecturer: Jenifer Ruiz-Valenzuela. Jenifer is an Associate Professor at the University of Barcelona and co-Director of the Public Policies Research Line at the Barcelona Institute of Economics (IEB). She is also a Research Associate at the CEP at LSE. Her research spans the Economics of Education, Labour Economics, and Public Economics. Known for her engaging communication style, Jenifer is a highly effective speaker in both academic and other public spheres. Presentations are a central component of the PhD journey, shaping how research projects are conveyed, evaluated, refined, and disseminated through seminars, workshops, conferences, the job market, and beyond. This lecture covers the various phases of preparing and delivering an academic talk, as well as how to benefit from one. It also extends beyond standard presentations to address other common formats, such as posters, discussant roles, elevator pitches, and interactions with the media. Contents of this lecture: Start Presenting Now Before the Talk: Design and Rehearse Deliver the Presentation Benefit from Academic Talks Other Presentation Formats Public speaking is a core skill for an academic. You need to sell your research, much like a vendor selling tomatoes at a supermarket. Presenting your findings to fellow economists or other interested audiences is an essential part of that process. While some academics are uneasy with this framing, selling in this context is not about exaggeration or marketing tricks. Rather, it is about giving the audience the information they need to understand the contribution of the paper and to see why the results matter. Therefore, pursuing a PhD is not just about producing rigorous analysis and novel results; one must also obtain the ability to communicate them clearly, convincingly, and confidently to a wide range of audiences. The success of a project depends not only on its technical merits but also on how well it is conveyed. This lecture provides practical guidance on preparing, delivering, and benefiting from academic presentations throughout the PhD and beyond.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: It is never too early to start giving presentations. Internal presentations, such as “work-in-progress” seminars in your department, can and should start as soon as a researcher has a research idea. These early talks do not require polished results, let alone a complete paper. Their purpose is to practice explaining the idea, clarify the intuition behind the strategy, and receive feedback that can help push the project forward. Presenting unfinished work internally is one of the most effective ways to learn how others perceive the project and where confusion arises. External talks, including conferences, workshops, and invited seminars (later in the career, of course), impose higher standards. In these settings, you need a story to sell, and the project should be quite polished, even if the analysis is not completely final. First impressions matter, and there is only one chance to give a first impression. For this reason, it is advisable to present externally only once the core idea, data, and empirical strategy are well developed and defensible. Over time, as you gain experience and confidence, these standards naturally become easier to meet. Applying to conferences can be a useful commitment device, forcing progress toward a deadline. It is also a tool to examine the readiness of the work for external presentations. However, submitting work that is not sufficiently developed could be counterproductive. A good rule of thumb is: results do not need to be written up perfectly, but they should exist clearly and robustly in the analysis. It is worth noting that Job Market Paper presentations require particular care. The appropriate level of polish depends on who is in the room. If potential employers are present, the paper must be highly refined, and you must be able to defend all aspects of the work. At the same time, Job Market Papers benefit enormously from being presented many times beforehand in “low-stake” settings, either internally or external student workshops, and with close coordination and feedback from advisors.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
section: Before the Talk: Design Slides and Rehearse
text: When preparing for the talk, remember that you are a seller. People would want to buy your product if they feel they understand it and see its value. As Rafe Meager puts it: “You must give people the information they need to understand the results you will show them, and to see why the results matter.”

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Slides play a supporting role in academic presentations. Their purpose is not to store all relevant information, but to guide the audience through the argument and to reinforce the speaker’s explanation. Well-designed slides reduce cognitive load, help listeners remain oriented, and make it easier to follow the logical structure of the talk. A fundamental principle of slide design is simplicity. That is, each slide should convey a single idea as clearly as possible. Try to write at most one line per point. You should absolutely not clutter slides. Put as little information as possible to convey the point. Overly dense slides or long blocks of text quickly overwhelm the audience and make it difficult to understand where the presentation is going. As a rule of thumb, if a slide feels crowded, it should be split into two. If an idea requires substantial explanation, it should be delivered verbally rather than written out in full. Also, avoid typos! When designing slides, visual emphasis should be used sparingly and consistently. A clear visual hierarchy, selective use of bold text, and restrained use of color help emphasize key messages without distracting from the content. Remember, emphasizing everything is emphasizing nothing. Whenever possible, use graphs over tables for communicating results. Visualizations allow audiences to grasp patterns, magnitudes, and dynamics at a glance, something that is difficult to achieve with dense regression tables. If tables are necessary, they should be adapted for presentation to be readable during the talk (from a distance without effort!). What you should not do is simply copy-paste the whole table from your working paper. Presentation tables should show only crucial information, such as the main point estimates, control summary ticks, and the number of observations.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Whether to include an outline slide depends on the context. In short talks like conference presentations, an outline is often unnecessary and can consume valuable time. In longer seminars or talks with unconventional structures, especially when having multiple methodologies or distinct sets of outcomes, an outline can help the audience stay oriented or highlight mechanisms. Besides, a brief preview of the main results can be useful in long talks, especially if there is a risk of running out of time. For literature slides, the goal is not to provide a comprehensive survey, but to situate the paper in the current literature. Therefore, you should only include those very related papers. Highlighting how you differ from existing studies (i.e., your contribution to the literature) is far more important than listing many citations. Since credibility is a primary concern for academic audiences, robustness checks are a common component of any presentation. Core robustness exercises should therefore appear in the main slides, integrated naturally into the narrative. At the same time, not all robustness checks need to be shown upfront. Additional analyses can be placed in backup slides and used selectively when questions arise. When presenting models in empirical work, simplicity and clarity are crucial: assumptions should be stated explicitly, technical jargon should be minimized, and theoretical predictions should be clearly linked to the empirical analysis.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: 1) Why should I rehearse? Rehearsing a presentation is essential because it substantially improves the quality of the talk. From the perspective of the audience, preparedness shows that you take the presentation seriously and signals respect for the attendees. People do not want to waste their time sitting there for a poor presentation. For you, the presenter, if you rehearse well, you will feel more confident and less anxious during the talk. You will rely less on the slides; you will read less and explain more, and engage more naturally with the audience. With enough rehearsal, you will also be able to use more precise language, making arguments clearer and more convincing. It helps identify weaknesses in the narrative, unclear transitions, or unclear intuition. Still, you will make mistakes, but fewer and smaller ones with rehearsals. 2) How can I rehearse? Rehearsing by yourself is the first and most important step. Timing the presentation, recording it, and observing one’s own delivery can be extremely informative. You will be able to notice any distracting body language, like arms crossed and hands in pockets. It also helps to detect excessive use of filler words and unclear explanations. For non-native English speakers, rehearsal is particularly valuable for practicing the pronunciation of frequently used terms not natural in their native tongue. Video conferencing tools can be helpful at this stage, as transcripts can reveal repeated phrases or sections that are difficult to follow. Practicing with your PhD colleagues is usually a helpful next step once you have mastered the individual rehearsal. Feedback from peers frequently highlights points of confusion that you may not anticipate and helps refine both content and delivery. Besides, as PhD students, providing detailed feedback for one another during these internal practices is a powerful way to foster mutual support and improve your presentation deliveries. Presenting in internal work-in-progress seminars provides additional benefits. You would want to invite more senior researchers to attend your internal talk and hear what they think about your project. Constructive criticism from faculty members is an important input into improving the quality of the presentation. Finally, the intensity of rehearsal should depend on the importance of the talk. For high-stakes presentations, such as Job Market talks, a stricter rehearsal discipline can be useful. Restarting the presentation from the beginning after a significant mistake reinforces fluency, sharpens transitions, and helps ensure a smooth and confident delivery.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Knowing the audience is critical. This is especially useful when designing the motivation slides. More specialized audiences, such as in a field-specific workshop, require a targeted motivation that dives quickly into the contribution, while a more general audience requires a broader “big picture” hook. Later in the career, when invited to give departmental seminars, it is often helpful to check the websites of the department and faculty members to understand the background of likely attendees. Practical considerations also matter. First, clarifying logistical details in advance, such as the total time allocated, whether questions are taken during or after the talk, and how time warnings are given, reduces uncertainty and anxiety. It is also important to pay attention to dress codes. In general, you should neither be dressed too casually nor too formally. Try to strike a balance: avoid wearing either sweatpants or full suits (except for Job Market talks, where suits are less out of place). Lastly, in some talks, you might need to bring water, a pointer, and a backup of your presentation on a USB drive. These small details can all contribute to a smoother experience.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Calm down, you’ve got this! It is important to remind yourself that you are the person who knows the most about your paper. Before your presentation starts, depending on the setting, you can try to have some minutes for yourself, go to the toilet, and motivate yourself. In the first few minutes at the beginning of the presentation, you will feel the greatest nervousness. Here are some tips to handle this: Use the title slide wisely to calm down. Thank the person keeping track of the seminar and the audience. Briefly introduce yourself and co-authors. Explain in a couple of sentences what the paper is about.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Do not start with an apology: try to inspire confidence. Confidence is conveyed through posture, movement, and tone. You should avoid standing still in front of the slides. Instead, move your body naturally, use your hands, and speak clearly and at a measured pace. A little reminder: do not use a pen that you can click on and off. Academic presentation is a dialogue, not a monologue. You will need to interact with the audience. The basics are to look at your audience and talk to them, not at your slides or the air. In order to keep them engaged, make sure that you speak loudly enough so that people in the back of the room can hear you clearly without effort, and do not talk too fast. Also, be careful with jokes. A spontaneous light joke is fine, but you don’t want to offend someone or make the talk unprofessional with edgy jokes. Finally, be a careful tour guide for your project. Important concepts should be explained clearly from the moment you mention them; never assume a concept is self-explanatory. When figures or tables appear, you should actively guide the audience through what they are seeing and why it matters.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Questions are an integral part of academic presentations. The mindset should be: Questions are good, they make your research better. When handling questions, make sure you first listen and then reply. Besides, it is often helpful to take brief notes on important comments (or ask someone to do it for you). 1) Listening. Questions should be approached with openness rather than fear. All questions are important; don’t dismiss any. When listening to the question, you should look at the person and nod with your head, just to show that you are actively paying attention. Questions should not be interrupted; wait until the question is over to reply. 2) Replying. Don’t start with “It’s a good point” in every answer. Even though you don’t want to dismiss any question, not every question reflects a valid concern. If a question will be addressed in the upcoming slides, it is appropriate to say so and postpone it. When unsure about an answer, it is better to acknowledge it by saying that you need to think more carefully about it. Be careful with extra-long answers when you feel too comfortable. Defending your work (especially your identification and model) is both legitimate and expected; argue nicely why you don’t agree with certain points made by the audience, and do not get defensive. If there is criticism, it’s of the project, not about you. It is possible to have a pushy attendee in the audience, you can always say “This is important, but if you don’t mind, we can continue the conversation after the presentation,” when they won’t let a point go.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Use a watch or a timer on the phone to keep track of the time. You can also kindly ask the chair/organizer or a colleague to give you a signal when you have, say, 10 or 5 minutes left. Even though you have prepared a lot, you might still run out of time. This can happen particularly if there are many questions. When this happens, the session chair or the seminar organizer might help pause questions for a few minutes so you can at least finish your main points. If you realize you are not going to make it to the end, do not try to rush quickly through all your slides. Instead, focus on presenting the most important and convincing results, ensuring that the narrative of the paper and its central contribution are clearly communicated.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: You’re not done (yet) when the presentation is finished! To make the most of your presentation, follow-ups are necessary. As a natural extension of the talk, you can try to reach out to the person who had any unfinished conversations or questions. Reach out also if you did not fully understand a comment. These can lead to productive exchanges or even future collaboration. Writing down a list of the comments as soon as possible helps preserve valuable feedback that might otherwise be forgotten. In the notes, you would want to explain the content of the comment and write down your answers, or try to look for them if you did not have an answer. After presenting 2 or 3 times, many comments reappear, and by taking notes and reflecting on them, you will perfect the answer to those questions! In some contexts, such as invited seminars or job market talks, it is appropriate and professional to send a brief thank-you email to the organizers.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Presenting research is only one side of academic exchange. Attending seminars and workshops effectively is equally important for learning, generating ideas, and building professional relationships. Academic talks provide exposure to new questions, methods, and perspectives, and they are a central setting in which researchers learn how others think, argue, and communicate. Simple habits, such as sitting in the front rows and minimizing distractions (put your phone away!), make it easier to focus during the presentation. Writing down some notes or key points helps understand the talk better (especially using old-fashioned notebooks). It is very natural to have doubts during the presentation. By asking questions, you can deepen understanding and contribute to the discussion, but it is important to pay attention and ensure not to ask repetitive questions. Most departments and research groups have a weekly seminar in your (loose) field featuring invited speakers from an external institution. Engaging with these speakers outside the formal presentation is often just as valuable as the talk itself. As a PhD student, you should try to sign up and talk to the speakers. When meeting with a speaker, introduce yourself as a PhD in a specific field. You can often discuss a research idea (motivation, identification, results). Productive conversations may also focus on questions you have about a paper by the speaker that you are interested in. Conferences and workshops also offer a great opportunity during breaks or meals to approach a presenter whose work interests you. Over time, regular exposure to cutting-edge academic presentations also sharpens your intuition about what makes a research question compelling and how strong arguments are constructed, and contributes to the development of your own research agenda. In this sense, benefiting from academic talks is not only about absorbing content and talking with presenters, but also about learning how good research is done and communicated.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: In addition to standard talks, there is a range of other formats of presentation. While the objectives and time constraints differ, all formats benefit from clarity, focus, and an awareness of the audience. 1) Posters. It’s all about the visuals. Poster presentation is a format in which you are more of a seller than in talks. Think of yourself again as a vendor standing in the market with your product while your potential audience passes by. Since interaction is often brief, you should choose wisely the main result and the main mechanism to include in your poster. At the beginning of the poster session, probably no one is stopping by. WHAT TO DO? You should try to make eye contact and smile at people walking by. Very likely, someone will then stop at your poster. To break the ice, you can start by asking whether they are interested in learning about the impact of X on Y. Again, very likely, people tend to be nice and say yes! If you manage to do so, the “contagion” starts, and other people will also stop by. 2) Discussions. Serving as a discussant requires a positive attitude and a constructive mindset. You don’t want to be the toxic element in the room! To make a good discussion, it is advisable to prepare a few slides, if allowed, or some clean and organized notes. This typically starts with a very brief summary of the paper before moving on to the discussion part, which typically includes: Pointing out the nice aspects. These could be, just to name a few, the contribution, the great data, innovative research design, or unexpected policy implications. Your contribution. You can flag potential robustness checks, suggest additional analyses (e.g., other outcomes or likely mechanisms), mention literature that could help the authors, discuss policy implications that were not mentioned, etc. Throughout, it is important to respect the allotted time and maintain a collegial tone. Remember, this is not your show, but to help others improve their projects. 3) Elevator pitches. This format is an extreme test of clarity. Pitches typically last no more than 30 to 60 seconds, or 100 to 150 words, if you draft them. You should avoid technical language and jargon at all costs. An effective elevator pitch: grabs the attention immediately by starting with a clear and engaging research question, explains what you are doing and why the question matters, states the main result in simple terms (answer to the question), ends with a hook or next step –something memorable or actionable. Practicing elevator pitches with non-academic audiences (your parents/grandparents, friends who are not economists, etc.) is a useful way to ensure that the core message of a project is truly clear.

title: Academic Talks in Economics
text: Engaging with the media is a whole other talk, even though some of the points in the previous sections are still valid. Media formats are often unfamiliar, time-limited, and less forgiving than academic settings. When contacted by the media, ask for questions in advance. And then you will prepare a lot for it. If you get any question unprepared for, bridge unexpected questions back to prepared messages (e.g., “This is a good point, but what I can tell you from my research is…”). Different formats, different strategies. Bring notes for recorded interviews and radio. Television appearances benefit from practicing body language and avoiding distracting clothing. Regardless of format, the guiding principle remains the same: clarity, preparation, and control of the message. The last piece of advice is always to ask any questions beforehand: time, microphone type, standing/seating, etc. This lecture discusses how to give an academic presentation and how to benefit from one. It is never too early to start presenting. When preparing for a talk, use a simple slide design and rehearse as much as possible. During the talk, be confident, interactive, and professional, and remember to handle questions with openness. Beyond presenting, junior researchers benefit from attending talks to shape good academic taste. Finally, mastering other formats of dissemination ensures research is effectively communicated throughout the PhD and beyond.

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: Lecturer: Albrecht Glitz. Albrecht is an Associate Professor at UPF and BSE, a Project Leader at RFBerlin, and a Research Fellow at CEPR, IZA, CESifo, and CReAM. His research spans Labor economics, migration, and the economics of espionage. Having supervised numerous PhD students and served repeatedly on hiring committees, Albrecht brings first-hand insight into how to craft a well-positioned Job Market Paper that signals the ability to produce independent and high-quality research. This lecture focuses on how to write the most important research product during the PhD journey: the Job Market Paper (JMP). The JMP is by far the most important item considered by prospective employers in the job market. During the PhD, one should focus their research efforts on the JMP. As a PhD Candidate entering the market, it is more important to have one finished JMP than many papers at earlier stages. In principle, the JMP should look like a paper in a top economics journal and should be written at the highest professional level for a wide audience of highly trained economists. This lecture is also helpful for writing other papers besides the JMP. Contents of this lecture: The Job Market Paper The Structure & Writing Guidelines Writing and Rewriting Final Remarks

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: While the PhD dissertation typically includes three related or unrelated papers as its chapters, the JMP is more than just a chapter and must stand alone as one self-contained, polished paper, written as if it could be submitted to a top journal. The primary purpose of JMP is to show that you can carry out a significant piece of independent research. It should be your most important written research product on the market; it should demonstrate originality, rigor, independence, and taste; it serves as a signal of your long-run research agenda. It is probably the only document that employers actually read before flyouts! When departments receive hundreds of applications, committees review dozens of applications under tight time constraints, and the Job Market Paper becomes the decisive factor in determining which candidates advance to interviews. Furthermore, departments read the JMP not only to evaluate the specific project but also to infer your trajectory as a researcher: what you have been able to do during your PhD is interpreted as a signal of what you will do in the years ahead. A successful JMP therefore has to have five elements: a clear and important question, a credible identification strategy or tight theoretical logic, a meaningful contribution relative to existing work, a clean exposition and professional presentation, and evidence that you can generate a stream of future papers.

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: Like all other research papers, a JMP includes a title, an abstract, an introduction, and a conclusion. The typical empirical and theoretical JMPs then differ in emphasis in their body parts. While this structure is typical, it’s not set in stone. Researchers may add sections when necessary (such as case studies), but should have good reasons for deviating from the standard format, as any deviation will draw attention from readers. An empirical JMP (Figure 1) typically begins with an introduction that lays out the research question, motivation, and contribution. It then provides a conceptual framework, along with the necessary context or institutional background. Following the description of the data, it describes the identification strategy and presents the main results. Subsequent sections explore mechanisms, heterogeneity, and robustness, before concluding with the broader implications. Technical details, proofs, and data cleaning are usually placed in an appendix, keeping the main text clean and accessible. Figure 1. Structure of an Empirical JMP Figure 2. Structure of a Theoretical JMP Figure 3. Structure of a Macro JMP A theoretical JMP (Figure 2) follows a similar logic but places more weight on the modeling section. After motivating the question and explaining its relevance, the paper typically provides an intuitive overview of the environment and key mechanisms before introducing the formal model. The formal section defines primitives, timing, assumptions, and equilibrium definition and characterization; subsequent sections develop the main results and comparative statics. Macro and structural JMPs (Figure 4) typically feature reduced-form empirical evidence, structural parameter estimation, model calibration, quantitative fit assessment, and counterfactual analysis. As with empirical papers, lengthy proofs belong in the appendix, while the main text focuses on clarity and intuition. Regardless of type, the unifying objective is clarity: A reader should never feel lost about the structure of the argument or the purpose of each section.

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: The abstract and the introduction are, by far, the most important parts of the Job Market Paper. They are the entry points to your work, the basis on which hiring committees form their first impressions. A strong JMP, therefore, should begin with a precise, disciplined, and persuasive opening. 1) The Abstract The abstract must communicate the essence of your paper in roughly one hundred words. Its role is not to summarize everything you do, but to make the reader understand immediately what the paper is about, what you do, what you find, and why it matters. A well-crafted abstract typically follows a clear structure: Start with the research question, stated plainly and without jargon. State what you do, mentioning the empirical strategy, theoretical framework, and setting. Present the main results with magnitudes: numbers matter here. Close with the key contribution and implications. Keep the abstract concise. It should be 5 to 7 sentences, or around 100 words. It should contain no vague statements. Background or literature lists should not be included, as the abstract is not the place to “set the stage” but the place to communicate content. Because of this, it should be written last, once the story of the paper is fully clear in your mind. Exercise 1: Analyze the abstract of your JMP (or one by someone else) according to the discussion above. 2) The Introduction The introduction is the most important section of the Job Market Paper because it’s often the only section that recruiters will read in detail before a flyout. Besides, the introduction is often the only section of a paper that people actually read after publication. Therefore, it needs to be edited and rewritten many times, and should be “perfect”. Keith Head provides a good structure for the introduction: The Hook. Open with a tension, a puzzle, or a stylized fact that makes the reader care. This is not decoration: it is your opportunity to demonstrate the economic relevance of the problem. (1 paragraph) Research Question. State clearly what the paper does. A sentence such as: “In this paper, I examine the effect of...” is often the most effective. Avoid vague descriptions or overly broad claims. (1 paragraph) Why It Matters. Explain the economic importance of the issue. This is where you situate the question in the broader policy or theoretical context. A reader should immediately understand the stakes. (1 paragraph) Literature Gap. Identify what previous work has not addressed. A typical formulation is: “While prior work has examined X and Y, we still know little about Z”. This gap creates space for your contribution. (1 paragraph) Contribution. Present your contributions clearly and explicitly. The standard format remains the most effective: “This paper makes three contributions.” Then list them in a logical order, each tied directly to the gap identified earlier. This paragraph tells the reader why your work should exist. (1 paragraph) Preview of methods and data. Offer a concise roadmap of your empirical or theoretical approach. This is the place to explain how you answer your question: which data, which variation, which model, and which key assumptions. Aim for clarity rather than technical completeness. (1-3 paragraphs) Preview of the main results. Present the central findings with magnitudes and economic interpretation. Numbers matter here: they anchor your contribution and give the reader a reference point for the rest of the paper. (1-2 paragraphs) Literature. Nowadays, literature is rarely isolated in a separate section; instead, it is integrated into the introduction and revisited where needed in later sections. Optional roadmap. Most papers end with a brief roadmap of the structure (“The rest of the paper proceeds as follows”). This is optional: many readers skip it, but it can be helpful if the paper is long or conceptually complex. Exercise 2: Compare two versions of an introduction paragraph, and tell why the second is better based on the discussion above. Version 1: Unemployment benefits are an important policy tool. In this paper, I discuss various aspects of unemployment insurance and present some empirical results. Version 2: This paper asks how unemployment benefits should vary across regions that differ in wages and housing costs. Using administrative data and a quasi-experimental reform in Germany, I show that a more spatially differentiated benefit system can improve welfare by X%. It is worthwhile to mention here the contribution and positioning of the paper. The recommended practice is to integrate the literature throughout, not only in one section. Strong JMPs weave positioning throughout the introduction and return to it whenever relevant in later sections, helping the reader understand continuously how the argument connects to and improves on what we already know. You must clearly state what is new in the paper and why that novelty matters for the broader field, and explain why your approach improves on existing work. The contribution should be tied directly to the identified literature gap. Precision matters when explaining the contribution. Overselling weakens credibility — readers quickly detect exaggerated claims or sweeping statements that cannot be supported. Underselling, however, obscures the value of your work and leaves the reader unsure why the paper should exist. Effective positioning strikes a balance: confident but careful, ambitious but precise.

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: For each of the other parts of the Job Market Paper, there are some key guidelines, both for keeping in mind when writing the first draft and as a checklist when revising the paper before releasing it. 1) Models and Theory For theoretical or structural JMPs, clarity in the modeling section is crucial. Before presenting any formal derivations, the reader must have a good understanding of the setup. This requires stating clearly the primitives, timing, and assumptions. It is essential to provide the economic intuition before formalizing. Notation should support the argument, not obscure it. A clear theoretical section demonstrates not only technical competence but also your ability to communicate complex ideas effectively. A well-written theory section offers a clear roadmap of the model, not just equations. The reader should understand why each assumption is made, how the components of the economic environment fit together, and what mechanisms the model is designed to isolate. Technical proofs and long derivations belong in the appendix, allowing the main text to highlight the economic mechanisms that drive the results. It is also worth noting that employers nowadays increasingly value seeing a (simple) theoretical framework even in primarily empirical papers, as it demonstrates that the author can think theoretically about their empirical analysis. 2) Data Section The data section should demonstrate that you take empirical work seriously and are meticulous in your approach. It should give a clear and coherent picture of the empirical environment, explaining in detail where the data come from, and what period and geographic unit they cover. Explain sample construction and selection criteria carefully and precisely: what observations are included or excluded, how key variables are defined, and which transformations (if any) are applied. When presenting descriptive statistics, it is often helpful to show the distribution of the main variables — through percentiles, density plots, or simple visualizations — so that the reader can understand the range, variation, and potential sources of heterogeneity in the data. These elements give context to the identification strategy and help the reader interpret the magnitude of the results. Descriptive statistics are also useful for us as researchers to identify potential data issues, such as detecting outliers. You should show variables as they appear in your analysis (e.g., changes rather than levels if your regressions use changes). Detailed coding decisions, cleaning steps, or complex construction procedures should be clearly documented, but reserved for an appendix or replication package to keep the main text accessible. By the end of this section, the reader should have complete confidence that the empirical analysis is built on a solid and transparent foundation. 3) Identification The identification section is the backbone of any empirical Job Market Paper. This is where you show the reader not only what you estimate but why the estimates can be interpreted causally. A strong identification section first describes, with clarity and precision, the source of variation that identifies the parameters of interest, be it a reform, an instrumental variable, a discontinuity, or an unexpected shock. A compelling identification section also requires stating your identifying assumptions explicitly. Then you should explain why assumptions are credible with supporting evidence. This is where balance checks, pre-trends, falsification, and placebo tests play a role. The goal is not to overwhelm the reader with tests, but to offer a set of targeted diagnostics that speak directly to the assumptions of the research design. If you use an IV, you should always report first-stage results to support its relevance. The last critical step in writing this section is acknowledging limitations. Acknowledging them shows maturity as a researcher. Every empirical strategy has weaknesses, and readers expect you to show that you have thought about them and explain how you address potential concerns. Often, limitations that seem fatal to young researchers are accepted by experienced readers if addressed honestly. 4) Presenting Results Once the empirical strategy is established, you will write your results to build a coherent narrative, with each table or figure advancing the story. The first step is to introduce the main specification and the core coefficients. After the main results, the narrative should unfold naturally. Mechanisms, heterogeneity, and alternative explanations are explored in separate but logically connected subsections. When writing the results, bear in mind that the emphasis should always remain on providing the economic magnitude of the estimates, not simply reporting numbers and statistical significance without translating them into meaningful economic terms. You should interpret signs, sizes, and mechanisms. Readers want to understand how large the effects are, why they arise, and whether they differ across relevant groups or contexts. If coefficients come with unexpected signs, they should be addressed, not ignored. If there are possible alternative explanations, you should address them systematically. A key suggestion in crafting the results section is to use clean, intuitive figures and tables. A good JMP should have figures and tables that can stand alone with comprehensive notes. They should be replicable from the information given, and fully labeled and clearly titled. Visualization greatly enhances this part of the paper, and a good figure can make a significant difference in how readers perceive your paper. When using figures, the principle is to use clean and intuitive visual design and minimize clutter. Tables should be used in a smart way: they should highlight the key coefficients rather than display every robustness check or specification. Avoid tiny fonts or too many decimals. Titles of the tables should state findings, instead of being just “Table 3”. 5) Mechanisms and Robustness A credible JMP does not stop at estimating a main effect; it seeks to explain the underlying mechanisms. This requires designing empirical tests that speak directly to the channels implied by the conceptual framework or the theory. Mechanism exercises help readers understand not only whether an effect exists, but why it arises and under what conditions it might be expected to appear. Robustness checks complement these exercises by showing that the results are not driven by artifacts. Strong papers approach robustness strategically: they test a focused set of plausible alternative specifications and address specific concerns with targeted tests, rather than using "kitchen sink" robustness checks. A good strategy to keep in mind in writing this part is to try to put yourself in the position of a potential referee, anticipate their concerns, preempt the 3-5 most likely referee objections, and then address these proactively in your paper. This is also to demonstrate that, as a strong job market candidate, you have thought about potential criticisms. 6) Conclusion Many conclusions simply repeat what was already explained in the paper. This should be avoided. A strong conclusion focuses on key takeaways, explains why they matter, and situates them within the larger debates or policy questions of the field. This is also the place to discuss the implications of the work — whether theoretical or policy-relevant — and to acknowledge limitations honestly. Besides, a brief but thoughtful suggestion for future research gives the paper a sense of openness and direction. The best conclusions leave the reader with a clear sense of contribution, relevance, and intellectual coherence, reinforcing why the project deserves to stand as a Job Market Paper.

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: In the end, writing a JMP is about communicating your findings effectively (in English). Good writing will help the reader identify the precise contributions of your paper, making life easy for your reader. Bad writing deters readers from finishing reading your JMP. But more to that, bad writing will be used as a negative signal about your skills as a researcher, since it often accompanies muddled thinking. This section first presents some language guidelines for writing the JMP, which are especially useful for non-native English speakers, and provides insights on how to improve the writing once you already have a draft.

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: A good writing style in economics rests on a few principles. First, an effective paragraph contains only one idea and follows a simple structure. It should begin with a clear topic sentence that clearly states the main point or claim that the paragraph will develop. A good strategy when writing a paragraph is to ask yourself: If I read only the first sentence, do I know what the paragraph is claiming? If not, the first sentence needs to be rewritten. Second, use short, direct sentences, and avoid “throat-clearing” phrases. Broad and vague openings such as “In recent years, there has been growing interest in…” or “The issue of X has become increasingly important…” add length to the sentence without adding any information. Also, use active voice, as it makes sentences more direct and easier to understand (Use “I show…” rather than “It is shown…”). Finally, at the word level, you should always remove unnecessary and filler words (indeed, very, somewhat). If you can take a word out without changing the meaning, take it out. Pay attention also to possible repetitions and avoid them. Besides, choose simple words over complex ones when they convey the same meaning. You should avoid acronyms and jargon, especially in the introduction. A reader encountering your work for the first time should not have to decode terminology before understanding the question. But whenever necessary, define terms immediately when used and stick to the terminology. Here is an example of a Jargon-heavy start: "Using a spatial RDD with a Bartik-shift instrument and an AKM value-added framework, I estimate the LATE of benefit variation on equilibrium outcomes.” A clearer version would be “Unemployment benefits are the same everywhere, yet living costs differ dramatically across regions. This paper asks whether benefits should vary with local prices.”

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: Good writing is rewriting, so expect many revisions. It is all about “molding a product” that changes constantly until it finally settles into its final form. Think of rewriting as a process. You should plan for multiple full passes through the paper: full re-evaluations of structure, flow, and clarity. Note that the introduction should be rewritten last, once the rest of the paper has stabilized. Another useful practice is to have your peers review your paper (and be tough with feedback). During the rewriting process, you will cut many pieces from the previous draft. It is important to maintain a “cut file” for removed text that might be useful later. Version control systems (even manually creating monthly copies of entire project folders) or a disciplined use of tracked changes help prevent chaos as the paper evolves. Presentations at internal workshops and seminars are opportunities to identify unclear aspects of your JMP that need improvement. If seminar audiences consistently get confused and ask clarifying questions about a particular part, that section of the JMP needs revision first. Common Mistakes Previous sections have set up good practices in writing the Job Market Paper. However, certain pitfalls recur frequently across JMPs. Reviewing them makes it easier to avoid them: Inflated motivation without a clear economic question. Long introductions with broad statements or policy background but no sharp research question leave readers unsure what the paper is actually about. Literature “dumping.” Excessive literature review that does not highlight your contribution. Again, strong JMPs “integrate” the literature to highlight the gap the paper fills. Overly technical exposition. Pages of algebra, formal notation, or econometric detail can overwhelm readers and obscure the underlying intuition. Technical material belongs in the appendix unless it is essential for understanding. Inconsistent variable names or notation across sections. Using different names for the same concept across sections confuses readers. Stick to your defined terminology. Burying the main result. When the key finding appears for the first time on page 25, the impact of the paper is lost. The main specification and central results should be presented early and clearly. Poor writing and repetitive content. This signals muddled thinking to employers. Spelling mistakes and grammatical errors suggest carelessness.

title: Crafting the Job Market Paper
text: The “Goldin–Katz ten rules” are a helpful summary of what makes a strong Job Market Paper, and echo with many of the points raised in this lecture: It is always possible to transform a good idea into a great JMP. The insights of your JMP will be judged by how you present them. Your JMP is an exercise in persuasion. No great paper first emerged from the author’s printer in that form. No author can see all (or even most) of his or her writing errors. Most paragraphs have too many sentences, and most sentences have too many words. The “foot-in-the-door” parts of your written work are the abstract and introduction. Verbalizing your argument is more difficult than writing it. Be your own worst enemy. There are many other rules: See the Goldin and Katz (2009) original pdf file. Remember, your JMP is the most important component of your job market application. Treat it as your flagship project: choose a question you care about, develop it with rigor, and present it with clarity and precision. Clear structure and careful exposition are as crucial as the substance of your contribution. Rewrite repeatedly and seek honest, critical feedback. You should aim for a paper that a busy economist wants to finish reading.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Lecturer: Diego Puga. Diego is currently a Professor at CEMFI and a leading scholar in urban economics, economic geography, and international trade. His research has been published in top academic journals and has also served in editorial roles at several major journals. Beyond academia, Diego has been deeply involved in policy work at both national and international levels, and is currently a member of Spain’s Council of Economic Advisers. Throughout this Guide, we have learned how to navigate the research process, generate and refine ideas, organize the workflow, visualize findings, deliver presentations, and craft a Job Market Paper. This closing lecture ties these threads together by shifting the lens to building research products. A paper is one product among several; elevator pitches, presentations, job market talks, and policy briefs are all distinct outputs that a researcher must learn to craft. What unites them is that every product must convey a story based on credible research. This lecture first addresses how to select a research project promising to turn into a research product. It then covers various academic products according to their length (short versus long) and medium (written versus oral), showing how the same core elements scale and adapt across formats, and briefly discuss policy-oriented products. Contents of this lecture: Before the Product Academic Products: an Overview The Short Academic Product: Abstract and Elevator Pitch The Long Academic Product: Introduction and Seminar Spiel Policy-Oriented Products

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Building a research product starts with having a research project, but not every project translates into a compelling product. Before discussing various research products in economics, it is worth asking what characteristics make a project more promising than others and what we should do as projects evolve.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Be creative and daring. As a PhD student, your most important research product will be the Job Market Paper. From the experience of evaluating many job-market candidates, hiring committees are far more impressed by candidates who have a novel JMP, where they have tried to do something different, even if it is maybe rough on the edges and less polished, than by someone with a paper that is technically polished but makes only a marginal advance. Of course, difficult things can fail more likely. Trying to tackle a difficult question and succeeding only in part can still demonstrate originality, courage, and the potential to do important work, which can already be enough to earn a flyout. Even a completely failed project is a learning process. The person willing to tackle new and difficult things is someone who will sooner or later do something important. And that’s exactly what is valuable to show for a young researcher. To have a creative project, start with an actual research question, not with a method or a dataset. It is tempting to begin from a method you want to apply or a dataset you have gained access to, and that is fine as a starting point, but it is usually much more productive to let the question come first and then search for the tools and data that best serve it. Your motivation should come primarily from the real world rather than the literature. Typically, it would be things that interest you, and people really notice when you genuinely care about the research, the question, and the answer, or just doing something mechanical. Saying “people have done X and I will do it differently” is fine, but saying something concrete about the world and why it matters is always more compelling. Caring is two-sided. It is partly about excitement and partly about investing deeply: reading, thinking, and learning every detail of your context. This requires that you develop deep knowledge of your context, to know the ecosystem, and invest in that. Especially in applied fields like development, economic history, and labor economics, there is a tradition of researchers being deeply invested in institutional details. Superficial approaches like “I have this data and these regressions, but I have never been to that country” are increasingly common and increasingly penalized.

title: Research Products in Economics
section: Rethinking your Project: Mind the “History Trap”
text: Most research projects change substantially over time. The initial idea, the initial prototype of a project, is hardly ever the best. There is a solid reason behind: good research is about discovery. If you knew from the beginning exactly what you would end up doing, it probably would not be that surprising. We all acknowledge that progress usually comes from adjusting the approach, redefining the focus, or rethinking key choices along the way. However, probably the single biggest mistake researchers make is letting your product reflect the history of how you did the project. At some point, it is useful to stop refining the existing draft and instead rethink the paper from the reader’s perspective, asking how the story should be told if it were written from scratch. The antidote is a simple question: This is my result, this is my story. What is the best way to communicate this if I were to do it from scratch? And sometimes it is actually good to do it from the ground! For example, when writing a paper, this sometimes means setting the old introduction aside entirely, sketching a new structure, and only then recovering pieces from the previous version. This is important because it is easy to get trapped by the history of the thing. It’s easy to think about it only from your own point of view as someone who researched, as opposed to someone who is coming in for the first time and trying to understand what you’re up to. Therefore, keep an open eye and keep rethinking the project. Always ask yourself from time to time: “Is this the best thing I can do with this? Is this the right way to do it?” Always think of people who have seen this before: what’s the best way to tell them the story?

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Before diving into different research products, here are some additional suggestions. First, at this stage of the career, it’s important always to keep a balance between two things: breadth and steady progress. Intellectual breadth is important at this stage. Reading papers, attending seminars, and taking courses outside of your core area can generate ideas through unexpected connections across different things. At the same time, be realistic. Writing a good paper takes time. Eventually, you will finish your PhD and need to look for a job. By then, you will need a product to sell. Most researchers discover the “right version” of the paper through trial, error, and iteration. Besides, if you have some margin, even just several extra months, there will be time to really communicate your product and have it in a shape that people can understand. Finally, seek opportunities to collaborate. Working with other students or with senior faculty is enjoyable, educational, and exposes you to different ways of thinking. Early connections are important because they are likely to last for your career. You keep seeing the same people for years, and you work together, sometimes you don’t, but you still keep in touch and collaborate.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Every research product tells a story, and every story is told in multiple formats: the paper itself, seminar presentations, meetings with advisors, elevator conversations at conferences, poster sessions, meetings with visiting speakers, and eventually job-market interviews and talks. Each of these academic research products has its own special advantages and constraints, but they also share many elements. They differ along two dimensions: Length. A short product conveys the essence in under a minute of reading or speaking (roughly 100 words). A long product takes several minutes to read or deliver (roughly 2–3 pages, or the first few minutes of a talk). Medium. A written product (abstract, introduction) is polished prose that must work on the page without the author’s voice. A verbal conversational product (elevator pitch, seminar opening, job market spiel) must work in real time with interruptions, body language, and audience interaction. These two dimensions produce four cells: Written Oral Short Abstract Elevator pitch Long Introduction Presentation Opening / Job Market Talk The short and long versions are the primary axis. Within each, the written and oral versions are structurally parallel: the abstract is essentially the script for the elevator pitch, and the introduction is the blueprint for the seminar opening. They receive disproportionate attention compared to other parts in the paper or the presentation, because they often determine whether an audience engages further. Many principles for the written product extend naturally to oral and informal communication. Mastering one helps you master the other. The following sections take each row in turn, before briefly discussing some principles of the full, longest version: the paper. Later, we will also explore a parallel category, policy-oriented products, which sits outside the academic grid. Remember, these products are all about communicating your research. Some researchers treat communication as secondary, as “marketing” rather than “real research”. But communicating research is not a secondary or superficial task. It is an essential part of the research process. You are selling something you care about, something you trust, something you believe is good. If the author does not articulate that story, no one else is going to do it for you, and all of those months and years of effort working on a project will be lost.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Take the written format as an example. When you have your tables and figures, or your model and propositions, getting some words around that is relatively straightforward. Yet writing the abstract, the introduction, and the conclusion is much more difficult to do. But they are key because those are what people read first, and if you don’t do it well, it will also be what they read last. For this reason, it is important to devote time to drafting them right from the beginning. Even if they don’t say what the results are because we don’t know yet, the motivation is there, the question is there, and the methodology is there. This early draft serves a double purpose: it forces you to articulate what the project is about, and it ensures that the abstract exists from the start. Every time you write a section, come back to the abstract and the introduction, keep working on them, and redo and polish them. Every time you write another section of the paper, come back to the abstract and revise it. Same for their spoken counterparts. Every time you present the project, notice which phrasings land and which fall flat, and update accordingly. By the end, hopefully, they are well done as you have spent time on them, without having to rush the night before submission. As a reminder, it is tempting, especially in the final months before the job market, to keep adding robustness checks and extensions. Resist this. Of course, having a good paper with lots of extensions and robustness is important. The marginal return to a better-written, better-motivated, better-structured abstract is almost always higher than the marginal return to one more robustness check.

title: Research Products in Economics
section: The Short Academic Product: Abstract and Elevator Pitch
text: The abstract and the elevator pitch are two expressions of the same product. They are the most important piece of communication you will produce. The abstract is what sits on the cover page of the paper; the elevator pitch is what you say when someone at a conference asks “So what are you working on?” when you meet a visiting seminar speaker, or in the opening minutes of a job-market interview. In each case, you have roughly one minute and the same elements to deliver. The short product is your way through the door. It takes time, it takes practice, but because it is short and structured and always has the same elements, if you are disciplined in terms of knowing “this is roughly the words I have, these are the elements that I have”, it’s feasible to do it and to do it well. If it fails to engage, the opportunity to communicate the research is lost. Once you are in, you can spend time on the details. But again, you first need to get in.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Good abstracts are surprisingly rare. Even candidates who can explain their project clearly in a two-minute conversation often have abstracts that are too long, poorly structured, and hard to read. There used to be a rule, imposed by the Journal of Economic Literature when it collected abstracts from other journals, that abstracts could not exceed 100 words. Like the old character limit on social media platforms, this constraint was useful precisely because it forced researchers to distilltheir message to its essence. A practical approach is to draft a version of 150 to 200 words and then condense it. A strong short product, whether written or spoken, contains three elements: Purpose: a clear statement of the research question and its importance. Methodology: a brief description of the methodology used to address the question. Findings: a high-level summary of the main findings and why they matter. Because the structures are parallel, preparing one well prepares you for the other. A tightly written 100-word abstract almost reads itself aloud as a pitch. Conversely, if you can explain your project clearly in 60 seconds of speech, you have the raw material for a strong abstract. If you need more words, the message is not yet sharp enough. Examples: The best way to internalise what makes a good short product is to study well-crafted examples. The following four abstracts, drawn from different top journals, topics, and methods, all execute the three-element structure of a short academic product. The Welfare Effects of Transportation Infrastructure Improvements, Allen and Arkolakis (2022, REStud) Abstract: Each year in the US, hundreds of billions of dollars are spent on transportation infrastructure, and billions of hours are lost in traffic. We develop a quantitative general equilibrium spatial framework featuring endogenous transportation costs and traffic congestion and apply it to evaluate the welfare impact of transportation infrastructure improvements. Our approach yields analytical expressions for transportation costs between any two locations, the traffic along each link of the transportation network, and the equilibrium distribution of economic activity across the economy, each as a function of the underlying quality of infrastructure and the strength of traffic congestion. We characterize the properties of such an equilibrium and show how the framework can be combined with traffic data to evaluate the impact of improving any segment of the infrastructure network. Applying our framework to both the US highway network and the Seattle road network, we find highly variable returns to investment across different links in the respective transportation networks, highlighting the importance of well-targeted infrastructure investment. The abstract opens with a vivid motivation: Each year in the U.S., hundreds of billions of dollars are spent on transportation infrastructure, and billions of hours are lost in traffic. One sentence, and the reader knows why this matters. Then the method: a quantitative general equilibrium spatial framework with endogenous transportation costs and congestion. Lastly, the finding: highly variable returns to investment across different links, which immediately implies that careful analysis matters for policy. Purpose, methodology, findings: all present, all clear. The Political Economics of Green Transitions, Besley and Persson (2023, QJE) Abstract: Reducing the emissions of greenhouse gases may be almost impossible without a green transition—a substantial transformation of consumption and production patterns. To study such transitions, we propose a dynamic model, which differs from the common approach in economics in two ways. First, consumption patterns reflect not just changing prices and taxes, but changing values. Transitions of values and technologies create a dynamic complementarity that can help or hinder a green transition. Second, and unlike fictitious social planners, policy makers in democratic societies cannot commit to future policy paths, as they are subject to regular elections. We show that market failures and government failures can interact to prevent a welfare-increasing green transition from materializing or make an ongoing green transition too slow. They first present the motivation/hook: Reducing the emissions of greenhouse gases may be almost impossible without a green transition, where they define the term explicitly, ensuring every reader follows. Then the method: “a dynamic model” differing from the common approach in two specific ways (changing values, not just prices and taxes; democratic policymakers, not social planners), with the contribution relative to existing literature is woven into it. Lastly, the finding: market failures and government failures can interact to prevent or slow a welfare-increasing green transition. Production Networks, Geography, and Firm Performance, Bernard, Moxnes, and Saito (2019, JPE) Abstract: This paper examines the importance of buyer-supplier relationships for firm performance. We develop a model in which firms outsource tasks and search for suppliers. Lower search and outsourcing costs lead firms to search more and find better suppliers, which in turn drives down marginal costs. We test the theory by exploiting the opening of a high-speed train line in Japan, which lowered the cost of passenger travel but left shipping costs unchanged. Using an exhaustive data set on firms’ buyer-seller linkages, we find significant improvements in firm performance as well as the creation of buyer-seller links, consistent with the model. The first sentence states the paper’s purpose: This paper examines the importance of buyers and suppliers for firm performance. Again, one sentence, and you know exactly what the paper is about. Then it presents the method: combining a model of outsourcing and supplier search with a natural experiment, the opening of a high-speed train in Japan. Lastly, the finding: significant improvements in firm performance as well as the creation of buyer-seller links, consistent with the model. What Drives Media Slant? Evidence from U.S. Daily Newspapers, Gentzkow and Shapiro (2010, ECTA) Abstract: We construct a new index of media slant that measures the similarity of a news outlet’s language to that of a congressional Republican or Democrat. We estimate a model of newspaper demand that incorporates slant explicitly, estimate the slant that would be chosen if newspapers independently maximized their own profits, and compare these profit-maximizing points with firms’ actual choices. We find that readers have an economically significant preference for like-minded news. Firms respond strongly to consumer preferences, which account for roughly 20 percent of the variation in measured slant in our sample. By contrast, the identity of a newspaper’s owner explains far less of the variation in slant. Here, the novel measurement strategy is explained up front: an index comparing a news outlet’s language to that of congressional Republicans or Democrats. Then: a demand model that estimates profit-maximising slant. The key result is immediately memorable: consumer preferences account for over 20% of variation in slant, while owner identity explains far less. The abstract is short, yet the research question, the method, and the findings are all unambiguous. Across all four examples, you see a very clear format. The elements are always the same. First, some motivation and a question. Second, since you’re going to end up talking about what you find, it cannot be just pulling a rabbit out of a hat, but needs to be a research output that people can trust. So you need to give a hint about the methodology. And then finally, the findings, then the actual core results. Sometimes they give you a number, often none. So it’s a very high-level summary of the findings. Typically, it also contains a hint of why the research is important.

title: Research Products in Economics
section: The Long Academic Product: Introduction and Spiel
