text: The long product extends the short product into a richer, more structured argument. For the written format, this would be the introduction of a paper, which is the most important and most difficult section to write. In terms of oral communication, the opening minutes of a seminar serve the same function. Besides, in a job-market interview, where you typically enter a Zoom meeting with a panel, you will be asked to “tell us about your research”. The first bit of the job market spiel is also going to be similar.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Below are two well-known frameworks for structuring an introduction, both capturing the essential ingredients. Essentially, they have the same elements: attracting the reader’s interest, stating the research question clearly, situating the paper within prior work, explaining its contribution, and sometimes outlining the paper’s structure. Table 2. Two Canonical Formulae Element Keith Head’s Formula Don Cox’s “Big Five” 1 Hook Tell your research question immediately. 2 Question Justify its importance. 3 Antecedents Spell out the deficiencies in previous work. 4 Value Added Explain what you are doing that’s better. 5 Roadmap Summarize your results right up front. 1) Hook and Question There are two ways to structure the first part of the introduction. One way to go is to first give the hook, something that provides motivation, and then go to the specific. The second possibility is to start from the very specific, your research question, and then go broader and explain why it matters. Both work. A hook is used to grab people’s attention by telling them that the paper tackles something important. It is important to keep it short. But be aware that a very broad motivation (“inequality is important”) is not a hook or motivation; a narrow, vivid fact tied directly to your project is. Some researchers seem to be worried about revealing too much too early, but remember, you are not writing a mystery novel! For the question, people need to know explicitly what the paper is about in the first paragraph of the paper. A good way to write this is to start with one sentence and then go into more detail, because formulating the whole question should be longer, maybe one or two paragraphs. It’s important to separate the question from the answer, so make sure you fully state your question before you actually start answering it. 2) Answer: method, results, and takeaway After fully stating the question, you need to talk about your answer and how you reached it. Therefore, you need to build trust by explaining the method: the type of model, the data, the key source of variation, and the identification strategy. Then state the results, identifying one key takeaway the reader can remember. When doing so, do not be afraid of committing to a clear message. There will always be caveats, but the core takeaway should be unmistakable. Restrict yourself to one or two numbers; more detail belongs in the body. Aim to keep the full introduction to roughly two pages. 3) Literature and Contribution The third part of the introduction is devoted to positioning your paper in the literature. Discussion of prior work should be selective and purposeful. The goal is not to cite everything, but to establish the foundations for the paper’s contribution. Every reference should answer a question of the reader: What do I need to know about prior work so that I understand what is new about yours? References that do not serve this purpose can be mentioned later in the paper. You need to explain what is important about what people have done before, give credit where credit is due, but also make clear what the shortcomings are, especially shortcomings that you are going to address. If there is a closely related or similar paper that you need to differentiate yours from, the best person to do it is yourself. Do it explicitly as opposed to hiding it. Literature review and the contribution part often come together. A way to state contribution while giving credit to prior work could be: “They did this, which is very important for this reason. However, they had this shortcoming, and my research is new because I solved this problem”. Note that the contribution is different from the main findings. The findings are the results. Implicitly or explicitly, this is the place where you should give an argument for why the paper should be published. 4) Limitations and Roadmap No paper is the final word on something; there’s always going to be shortcomings. If there are shortcomings you cannot fully resolve, it is often better to acknowledge them in the introduction and explain why they should not be overly worrying, rather than simply ignoring them. You know the paper better than anybody; you can find the argument better. But keep the focus on the main issues, as the introduction is not the place to defend against every possible criticism. Typically, you finish the introduction with a roadmap. However, if the roadmap is very standard, such as “data, methodology, results, conclusions”, then you might skip it. If you have already described what you do very linearly, you can also skip it to avoid redundancy. Once you have a complete draft of the long product, perform a systematic coherence check. A well-written paper forms a coherent whole. The research question, the answer, and the discussion of prior work should reinforce one another. Useful consistency checks include asking yourself some questions: Does the motivation make readers care about your specific question? Does the answer really read as an answer to that question, or to a subtly different one? If a reader saw only the shortcomings you identify in prior work, would they already guess what your paper does? Does the description of your contribution match the gaps you outlined? Making sure all the pieces fit together.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: The long written product naturally extends beyond the introduction into the body and conclusion of the paper. While the abstract and introduction are the most difficult and highest-return sections to write, the rest of the manuscript also constitutes part of the research product and should be crafted accordingly. Paper structure Standard structures exist for empirical and theoretical papers. If you deviate, have a good reason, because readers will expect the convention. Applied empirical paper: Introduction → Background → Model/Empirical Strategy → Data → Results (possibly split into multiple sections) → Conclusion. Applied theory paper: Introduction → Motivating Evidence → Model → Results → Extensions → Evidence Supporting Model Implications → Conclusion. This “theory sandwich” is typical: motivating evidence informs the model, and the model generates additional predictions (difficult to come up with without the model) that are then tested empirically. In addition, in both oral and written forms, the pyramidal structure applies: bottom line up front, then details developing the argument, and finally background and supplemental information. In this way, you go from less to more. Notice that when we discussed both the short and long products, we already had this structure: bottom line up front (first state research question), details to develop the argument (answer), and then antecedents/contribution/roadmap are the background and context. This principle scales down to individual sections and even paragraphs: each paragraph should open with a topic sentence that previews its content. A useful exercise for the written products: take the first sentence of each paragraph in your introduction, read them in sequence, and check whether they read like a slightly longer abstract. Tables and figures Tables and figures are great for conveying results. They should be self-contained: clear titles, labeled axes, explicit variable names, estimation methods noted, and footnotes providing enough details that a reader can understand the exhibit without consulting the main text. Many readers browse a paper by reading the abstract, then the introduction, then skimming the tables and figures. If those elements do not stand alone, you lose that reader. Adapt tables and figures for different contexts. Tables in seminar slides should focus on the key variables. For figures, label curves directly rather than relying on external legends, and choose color-and-pattern combinations that remain legible in black and white. Theory Any model is a representation of reality with enough simplification to distill clear conclusions yet not so much that it becomes unrealistic or irrelevant. Therefore, you need a careful balance between simplicity and realism for your model. When you have a model, there will be many assumptions. Solow’s famous growth paper starts with “All theory depends on assumptions which are not quite true. That is what makes it a theory. The art of successful theorizing is to make the inevitable simplifying assumptions in such a way that the final results are not very sensitive. A ‘crucial’ assumption is one on which the conclusions do depend sensitively, and it is important that crucial assumptions be reasonably realistic.” Therefore, for every assumption, do two things: explain why it is there and what feature of reality it captures, and state whether it is made for analytical convenience or whether it is crucial for the results. If an assumption is crucial, provide evidence that it is realistic. Conclusions Keep conclusions short, typically one page. This is where you Summarize key takeaways and limitations, but also somewhere to have the liberty to be more speculative than in the rest of the paper. You can discuss policy implications, suggest directions for future research, or sketch how the project could be extended. While speculation is acceptable here, it still should be grounded in your research. Krugman discussed in his 1980 AER paper that allowing factor mobility might produce agglomeration, an idea that became the foundation of the New Economic Geography eleven years later. Of course, your speculations in the conclusion do not need to go this far, but it is still a good place to say that the work is part of a broader agenda, or to preempt criticism by highlighting how you could have tackled things that might worry people, which you are not doing but would reasonably not go against your research. Lastly, as an additional brief comment for producing research outputs. Nowadays, new tools such as artificial intelligence can assist with specific tasks, such as editing or improving clarity (and are super good for coding). A recommendable way of using AI for writing is to guide it carefully and use it to refine existing text, or when there is already a satisfying initial structure. Think of AI as a capable assistant that helps you think, code, and write more efficiently, not as a replacement for your own thinking and writing.

title: Research Products in Economics
text: Academic research products are not the only outputs an economist can produce. Policy-oriented research constitutes a parallel category with its own formats and constraints. Understanding these formats is valuable even at the PhD stage. Policymakers may seek research evidence to inform decisions, to justify actions already taken, or to improve implementation. There are roughly three types of policy-related research outputs: Policy Evaluation: Academic journals prioritise novelty, but policy-oriented research often requires answering a question for a concrete measure important for the decision. For instance, evaluating a transport program, a labor-market reform, or a tax change for a particular setting is a genuine input into the decision process. Therefore, even if they probably will not yield a top-journal publication, these papers are still valuable products. Advisory Input: Policymakers sometimes seek insights from researchers to inform decisions they have not yet made. This is probably going to happen later on in your career, such as taking the role of an Economic Advisor. For this, policymakers would want to talk to you and obtain information that you know about because you are a researcher. Therefore, producing this format of output involves identifying research informative for their decisions, and translating academic findings into accessible and actionable knowledge. Policy Justification: When policymakers have already decided on doing something, they will want to seek some justification and hope that you can provide some research to support it. This is more common than one might expect, but it varies greatly across countries. The boundary between academic and policy research is evolving. As data-driven analysis and more sophisticated exercises become more common within governments, the demand for economists who can do rigorous research in policy settings is growing. This means that policies are much better grounded in solid research, but it also has implications for your job-seeking process. For PhD students, the skills you develop, such as careful identification, transparent analysis, and clear communication, have value well beyond the walls of academia, but it also requires greater flexibility and adaptability of these skills in the policy domain.

title: Afterword
text: We never thought this would end up being such a public good. But here we are! The BESTEPS Guide grew out of the BESTEPS Lectures, a flagship PhD training project organized at the UB School of Economics (UBSE). But it is more than just a collection of lectures. Just as generating a research idea begins with identifying a relevant and answerable gap in our knowledge, designing the BESTEPS project followed the exact same logic. For us, the gap was a set of research skills missing from the standard PhD curriculum, skills that are not only practical but also sharpen the judgement and research sense that are more important than ever in the age of AI. Looking back, we are glad that we took up the opportunity and built a fully demand-driven curriculum to fill it. Such a curriculum, taught by leading experts, is too valuable to keep to ourselves. This Guide is our attempt to turn the lectures into a shareable resource, one that can lower the barriers for junior researchers around the world facing the same steep learning curves. It was not easy: we invested more than 100 hours turning it into what we hope is an enjoyable read. A project like BESTEPS does not appear in a vacuum. It needs a community that is at once rigorous and collaborative, and that takes early-career researchers seriously. Years of collective effort have made UBSE exactly such a place, with its PhD program playing a central role. Here, faculty and students work in close contact, junior researchers bring early-stage ideas to the biweekly “Brainstorm Coffees”, and PhD students organize seminars across universities in Barcelona. This is the UBSE that made BESTEPS possible. BESTEPS is, ultimately, an expression of this broader vision: we have seen what a research community can give to those just starting out, and we believe what it gives should not stay behind our own doors. This Guide is our small way of contributing to the wider academic community we belong to. The research journey is hard for all of us; wherever you are along the way, we hope the Guide meets you there. Mengwei Lin BESTEPS Coordinator & PhD Candidate University of Barcelona & IEB Jordi Roca Solanelles Head Manager, UBSE University of Barcelona
